323.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Sikh means by seva
323.hook: the first visit: a Sikh kitchen where nobody asks who you are
323.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Buddhist means by the breath
323.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, sweeping, and caring for shoes, and outside it through relief work; the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the three tracks ended. Karma, bhakti, jnana: serving, singing, asking, and all of them a doing. Which one did you do on purpose? This week, we visit the neighbors. Day three hundred twenty-three.
screen: `KARMA · BHAKTI · JNANA — ALL A DOING.`

segments.voice: This week is different. Every other door on this app, Sikh, Buddhist, Muslim, Jewish, Christian, Catholic, spent its first camp teaching its own first words. For seven days, you get to visit. One house a day. The rule for a guest is simple: you listen to how they say it, in their words, and you don't take it home and blend it into yours. First visit: a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship. Take off your shoes, cover your head, wash your hands. There's a kitchen at the back, and someone is already handing you a plate.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS, SEVEN VISITS.` → `LISTEN IN THEIR WORDS.` → `FIRST DOOR: A GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: Sit down on the floor, in a row, next to whoever's there. That kitchen is the langar, and the meal is free, to anyone, of any faith or none. Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru, and to the Gurus after him. Tradition tells that the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, asked everyone who came to see him to eat in the langar first, sitting in the same rows, and that even the emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate. Everyone at the same height. That's the first thing seva means in a Sikh home: service that erases rank. The second: it's done with your whole self. Sikhs often speak of three kinds: seva with the body, like cooking, sweeping or cleaning the shoes of the congregation; seva with the mind, like teaching or reciting; and seva with what you have, giving money or food. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, volunteers cook, serve and wash dishes for whoever comes, every day, and for them the washing up is a form of worship. The third: it has no bill. In the Sukhmani, a long hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in effect, that the one who serves without wanting anything back is the one who reaches the Master. Seva isn't a way to earn something. For Sikhs it's a way of remembering God with your hands. You've met the word seva before, on this path, on day fifteen. Hindus use it too. Today you heard it the way a Sikh says it, from a Sikh kitchen floor.
screen: `THE LANGAR: FREE, TO ANYONE.` · `EVERYONE AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `BODY, MIND AND WHAT YOU HAVE.` · `SERVICE WITH NO BILL.` · then, large: `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind one time somebody fed you, or served you, and asked nothing back. A parent, a stranger, a nurse, a friend with soup. See their hands. Breathe in, and let yourself be the guest for a moment. Breathe out, and notice what it felt like to receive without a bill. Nothing to repay. Just the plate being handed to you. The bell holds the time.
Seva, selfless service, as Sikhs say it: a kitchen floor where everyone eats at the same height, with your whole self, and no bill attached.

today's visit: `SEVA, AS SIKHS SAY IT.`

segments.voice: Your line: everyone at the same height. Today, serve one person with nothing attached: a refill, a dish, a door held. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Buddhist means by the breath
324.hook: the second visit: a Buddhist hall where the only instruction is to know you're breathing
324.carry: breathe the way you're already breathing
324.tomorrow: guided visits: what the Sufis mean by remembrance
324.howItsDone: Many Buddhists, in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike, practice mindfulness of breathing, sitting quietly and knowing each breath as it comes and goes, often in a hall with a bell to begin and end.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first visit: a Sikh kitchen, and seva with no bill. The strand's name for this week, what a Buddhist means by the breath, becomes today's visit. Did you serve someone with nothing attached? Day three hundred twenty-four.
screen: `SEVA, AS SIKHS SAY IT.`

segments.voice: Second visit. A Buddhist meditation hall: a wooden floor, cushions in rows, a bell, a small statue of the Buddha at the front. You expect instructions. Relax your shoulders. Breathe in for four, hold for four. Picture a light. The teacher says none of that. She says: sit. Breathe the way you're already breathing. And know it. That's all? That's all. And people have spent their whole lives inside that one instruction. Today, the breath as the Buddhists who kept it for twenty-five centuries mean it.
screen: `A HALL, A BELL, CUSHIONS.` → `NO COUNTING, NO PICTURE.` → `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: The teaching comes from a discourse Buddhists call the Anapanasati Sutta, mindfulness of breathing, in the middle-length collection of the Buddha's talks. It begins almost like stage directions. A monk goes to the forest, or the root of a tree, or an empty hut. He sits with his legs crossed and his back straight, and sets mindfulness in front of him. Then, mindful, he breathes in. Mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in a long breath, he knows: I breathe in long. Breathing in a short breath, he knows: I breathe in short. That's the first surprise. Nothing is being fixed. The long breath isn't better than the short one. The practice is knowing, not steering. The second surprise is how far it goes. The sutta lays out sixteen steps. They start with the length of the breath, move through the whole body calming, then feelings, then the mind itself, and end with watching everything change and letting go. The Buddha says, in that text, that this one practice, developed, brings the four foundations of mindfulness to completion. One breath, and the whole path is folded inside it. The third: why the breath? Because it's always here, and because it never stays. Each breath is gone as it arrives. Buddhists call that anicca, impermanence, and the breath teaches it every four seconds without saying a word. The Buddhist door made the breath its second word, on day two. A guest's job today is just to hear it their way: not a technique for power, but a place to know what's happening, right now.
screen: `MINDFUL, HE BREATHES IN.` · `KNOWING, NOT STEERING.` · `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.` · `EACH BREATH GONE AS IT ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: This one is simple to say. Sit, back straight, the way the text describes. Don't change the breath. Just know it. When a breath comes in long, notice: long. When it comes in short, notice: short. When your mind wanders off, and it will, notice that too, and come back to the next breath. No counting, no picture, no goal. Just a guest sitting quietly in someone else's hall. The bell holds the time.
Anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out. Not controlling it; knowing it, and watching it change.
screen: `ANAPANASATI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breathe the way you're already breathing. Today, three times, catch one breath and just know it: long or short. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what the Sufis mean by remembrance
325.hook: the third visit: a circle of people saying one line until the room goes quiet inside
325.carry: polish the heart like a mirror
325.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Jew means by Shabbat
325.howItsDone: Muslims do dhikr alone, often after the daily prayers on fingers or prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather in circles to repeat a phrase such as la ilaha illallah together, and the Mevlevi order performs a turning ceremony.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: anapanasati. Not steering it, just knowing it, long or short. Did you catch one breath and simply know it? Today, a third house. Day three hundred twenty-five.
screen: `THE BREATH — KNOWING, NOT STEERING.`

segments.voice: Third visit. It's late on a Thursday night, in a room with carpets on the floor. Twenty people sit in a circle, some old, some young, a few with their eyes closed. Someone begins a line in Arabic, softly. The circle picks it up. The same few words, again and again, a little louder, then softer, the heads moving gently with the rhythm, until the words sound less like speech and more like breathing. You might have seen a clip of whirling dervishes in white skirts and tall hats. This is their family, and it's about something quieter than the spinning. Today, what the Sufis mean by remembrance.
screen: `A CIRCLE, LATE ON A THURSDAY.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `WHAT THE SUFIS MEAN BY REMEMBRANCE.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is dhikr. It means remembering, and it also means mentioning: saying the name out loud. The Islamic door taught it as one of its first words, and it belongs to all Muslims, not only Sufis. A Muslim who whispers subhanallah or alhamdulillah after prayer is doing dhikr. The Qur'an puts it simply. In Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" And in another place God says, remember Me, and I will remember you. Sufis are Muslims who give their lives to that line about the heart. Sufism isn't a separate religion; it's a path inside Islam, with teachers, lineages and circles, often called orders. Many of them gather for dhikr together, repeating a phrase like la ilaha illallah, there is no god but God, many times over, sometimes with the breath, sometimes silently in the heart. The Mevlevi order, founded after the poet Rumi, turns the remembrance into a slow turning dance. Why repeat? A Sufi would say: because the heart forgets. Not out of wickedness, just out of busyness. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Bukhari's collection to have said that the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. Dhikr polishes the heart, Sufis say, the way you'd polish a mirror, until it can reflect what it's facing. Muslims don't all agree about every Sufi practice; some question the music or the dancing. The heart of it is in the Qur'an itself: in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.
screen: `DHIKR: REMEMBERING, MENTIONING.` · `IN THE REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `A CIRCLE, ONE PHRASE, AGAIN.` · `POLISHING THE MIRROR.` · then, large: `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: You're a guest in the circle, so no one expects you to say their words. Just sit and listen to the rhythm of your own breath, the way the circle listens to its line. Notice how often, in two minutes, the mind forgets where it is and wanders off. Each time you notice, come back. That coming back is the movement a Sufi calls remembering. If you are a Muslim, you can let a phrase you already say ride quietly on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr, remembrance, the heart coming back to God, again and again.

today's visit: `DHIKR, AS SUFIS SAY IT.`

326.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Jew means by Shabbat
326.hook: the fourth visit: a Friday table, two candles, and a day that stops the week
326.carry: a day made holy by stopping
326.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Christian means by grace
326.howItsDone: Jews welcome Shabbat at sundown on Friday by lighting candles and blessing wine and bread, rest through Saturday with prayer, meals and family, and close it at nightfall with havdalah; how strictly work is set aside differs among Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and other Jews.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: The strand still reads dhikr, but yesterday's house was a Sufi circle: dhikr, the heart remembering, again and again. Did you catch yourself coming back? Day three hundred twenty-six.
screen: `DHIKR — THE HEART COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Fourth visit. Friday, just before sunset. A kitchen that's been busy all afternoon goes suddenly still. The table has a white cloth, two braided loaves under a cover, a cup of wine or grape juice. Someone strikes a match and lights two candles, then draws her hands in toward her face and covers her eyes. Phones go face down, or away entirely, until Saturday night. From here to nightfall tomorrow, this house is keeping a day the Torah sets apart on its first page. Today, what a Jew means by Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST BEFORE SUNSET.` → `TWO CANDLES, TWO LOAVES.` → `WHAT A JEW MEANS BY SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root that means to stop, to cease. It begins on the first page of the Torah. After six days of making the world, the text says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing the Bible makes holy isn't a place or a person. It's a day. Later, the Ten Commandments give Shabbat twice, with two different verbs. In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: observe it. Remember and observe. Jewish tradition says God spoke both words at once, and some families say that's why there are two candles. Remember is the inside of the day: rest, blessing, the meal, the singing, time with the people at the table. Observe is the outside: the things you don't do. In Orthodox homes that means refraining from thirty-nine kinds of creative work the rabbis listed, from writing to kindling a fire; many Jews keep the day in other ways, with different lines, and the movements differ on how. What they share is the stop. Heschel described Shabbat as a kind of palace built in time rather than space: a cathedral you can't visit, only enter, once a week. And the day ends the way it began, with a flame: a braided candle at Saturday nightfall, a sweet smell of spices, a blessing called havdalah, separation, and the week starts again. The Jewish door taught Shabbat as its third word. A guest's job today was to hear it their way: not a day off, but a day made holy.
screen: `SHABBAT: TO STOP.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `REMEMBER AND OBSERVE.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Take the next two minutes as a very small stop. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Let your hands be still, the way they'd be once a candle is lit. Let the list of unfinished things stay unfinished; it will still be there at the bell. Breathe in: stop. Breathe out: rest. A guest at someone else's table, keeping quiet while they keep their day. The bell holds the time.
Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, the seventh day made holy.

327.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Christian means by grace
327.hook: the fifth visit: a song everyone knows, written by a man who didn't think he deserved to sing it
327.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Catholic means by the rosary
327.howItsDone: Christians speak of grace in sermons, hymns and prayers, and many say grace before meals; Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive grace especially through the sacraments, while many Protestants emphasize grace received through faith.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: The strand's name is still Shabbat, and yesterday's house kept Shabbat: a day made holy by stopping. Did you find ten minutes where nothing got finished? Day three hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `SHABBAT — A DAY MADE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Fifth visit. A church, any church: stone or strip mall, a choir or a guitar. Sooner or later someone starts a song that long ago walked out of church and into the wider world. Amazing grace, how sweet the sound. It was published in England in 1779, by John Newton, a clergyman who had once worked in the Atlantic slave trade, and who later, publicly, turned against it. When he wrote about a grace that saved a wretch, he wasn't being modest. He meant it. Today, what a Christian means by grace.
screen: `A SONG THAT LEFT THE CHURCH.` → `JOHN NEWTON, 1779.` → `WHAT A CHRISTIAN MEANS BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament's word is Greek: charis. It means a gift, a favor, something given freely, and it sits in a family of words about joy and thanks. That's the first thing grace means for Christians: a gift you didn't earn. Paul puts it plainly in his letter to the Ephesians. In the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not a wage. A gift. The second thing: grace finds people at their weakest, not their best. Paul writes that he begged the Lord three times to take away something he calls a thorn in the flesh, and heard this answer: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." That's why Newton could sing it. Grace, for Christians, isn't a prize for the ones who got it right. It's what meets the ones who didn't. The third thing: Christians differ on how grace works, and they say so. Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that grace comes especially through the sacraments, like baptism and communion, and that a person freely cooperates with it. Many Protestants, following the Reformation, stress grace alone: salvation as God's gift, received by faith, with good works flowing from it rather than earning it. Different accounts, one word at the center. And it turns up at ordinary tables too. When a family says grace before a meal, the phrase comes down from the Latin for thanks. The Christian door taught grace as its second word, and the Catholic door as its first. A guest's job today was just to hear it their way: love you didn't earn, and can't.
screen: `CHARIS: A GIFT, FREELY GIVEN.` · `NOT A WAGE.` · `STRENGTH MADE PERFECT IN WEAKNESS.` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON HOW IT WORKS.` · then, large: `GRACE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one good thing in your life you didn't earn. Not your job, not your effort. Something given: a friend who stayed, a morning you woke up well, a person who forgave you before you asked. Breathe in, and let yourself receive it without explaining why you deserve it. Breathe out, and notice what that's like. If you pray, you can say thank you in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Charis, a gift, a favor, freely given, love that isn't earned.

328.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Catholic means by the rosary
328.hook: the sixth visit: a grandmother's beads, and a garden of roses you can hold in one hand
328.carry: beads in the hand, a story in the heart
328.tomorrow: guided visits: the light in me sees the light in you
328.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, in homes, churches and at bedsides, moving through five decades of Hail Marys on a string of beads while meditating on the joyful, sorrowful, glorious or luminous mysteries.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: The strand still says charis; yesterday's house said grace: a gift freely given, love that isn't earned. Did you give one small thing nobody had to earn? Day three hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `GRACE — A GIFT, FREELY GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Sixth visit. A hospital waiting room at two in the morning. An older woman in a cardigan sits very still, and in her lap her fingers are moving, one bead, then the next, her lips barely stirring. She isn't reading anything. She isn't looking at her phone. She's been doing this for an hour and she'll do it for another if she has to. If you've ever counted japa on a mala, you'll recognize a hand like that. But this is someone else's house, with its own words. Today, what a Catholic means by the rosary.
screen: `A WAITING ROOM, 2AM.` → `FINGERS MOVING, BEAD BY BEAD.` → `WHAT A CATHOLIC MEANS BY THE ROSARY.`

segments.voice: The name comes from the Latin rosarium: a rose garden. Tradition pictures each prayer as a rose, and the whole string as a garden offered to Mary, the mother of Jesus. The shape is simple. The circle of beads holds five decades, groups of ten. Each decade begins with the Our Father, the prayer Jesus taught, then ten Hail Marys, then a short praise called the Glory Be. The Hail Mary is built mostly from the Gospel of Luke. The angel's greeting, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." And her cousin Elizabeth's words: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." The second half of the prayer, asking Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death, was added by the Church over the centuries. The beads aren't the point; they keep count so the mind can go somewhere else. With each decade, Catholics meditate on a scene, called a mystery, from the lives of Jesus and Mary: the joyful ones, like the birth in Bethlehem; the sorrowful ones, the passion and the cross; the glorious ones, the resurrection. In 2002 Pope John Paul II added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. So the lips are saying one thing while the heart walks through a story. Catholics honor Mary and ask her prayers; they worship God alone, which is why the prayer asks her to pray for us. The Catholic door taught the rosary in two days, the beads and then the Hail Mary. A guest's job was simply to hear it their way.

segments.voice: No beads needed. Rest one hand in your lap, and let your fingers touch, thumb to fingertip, one finger at a time, slowly, again and again, with the breath. Let the hand keep the count so the mind doesn't have to. Then let one scene from someone's life, a birth, a hard day, a morning something came back, walk quietly through your mind while the fingers move. If you're Catholic, you can say the Hail Mary. The bell holds the time.
Rosarium, a rose garden. Beads counted in the hand while the heart walks through the mysteries of Jesus and Mary.

segments.voice: The strand's name for the week, rosarium, has held six visits. Yesterday's was the rosary: beads in the hand, a story in the heart. Did your fingers keep a quiet count? Day three hundred twenty-nine.

segments.voice: Last visit of the week, and it starts at home. Day one of this whole path, three hundred twenty-eight days ago, your first word was namaste. Palms together, a small bow. And your very first carry: the light in me sees the light in you. You've carried it for most of a year. This week you've been a guest in six other houses. It turns out the idea underneath that line lives, in different clothes, in other houses too. Today, the last guided visit: what that line sounds like when other people say it, in their own words.
screen: `DAY ONE: NAMASTE.` → `YOUR FIRST LINE: THE LIGHT IN YOU.` → `OTHER HOUSES, THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start at your own door. Namaste is namah, a bow, plus te, to you. I bow to you. That's what the syllables say. The light-in-me line is what the bow means: many Hindus say you bow to the divine in the other person, the same atman you met on day ten. The words are the bow; the line is the reason for it. Now the neighbors, one at a time, each in their own words. The Jewish house begins on the Bible's first page. In the 1917 translation: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him." Every human face, Jews say, carries that image. One rabbi in the midrash warns that whoever puts another person to shame should remember whose likeness they are shaming. The Sikh house has a hymn sung every evening in many gurdwaras, the Aarti of Guru Nanak, which says, in effect, that one Light is in everyone, and that Light is God's. The Quakers, a Christian community, have a phrase from their founder George Fox in the 1600s: to answer that of God in everyone. Quakers still use it to explain why they don't bow to titles, and why they sit in silence together. These aren't one teaching wearing four costumes. A Jew, a Sikh, a Quaker and a Hindu would each explain their line differently, and each would want to be heard in their own words. That was this week's whole rule. But from your door, you can notice something: in many houses, people have looked at the person in front of them and seen more than a person. Seva, the breath, dhikr, Shabbat, grace, the rosary. Six houses, and now one bow.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the faces from this week's visits: the woman ladling dal, the teacher saying just know it, the Sufi circle, the family lighting candles, the choir, the grandmother with beads. Don't blend them. Let each one be itself. Then, if you like, bring your palms together and give each a small bow in your mind, one at a time. Then one more, for the next person you'll see today. The bell holds the time.
Namaste, I bow to you. The strand's name for the whole week of visits comes home: namaste, and the light other houses see in a face.
